claims.text: The precise Pt–Ru ratio controls reduction kinetics during secondary heating.
The precise Pt–Ru ratio controls local atomic mixing during secondary heating.
Reduction kinetics and local atomic mixing govern whether a single-phase solid solution or phase-separated material forms.
The spray-dried precursor has nanodomain heterogeneities arising from atomistic mixing.
Systematic variation of the Pt–Ru ratio under controlled secondary heating can modulate decomposition and reduction kinetics.
Sufficiently high Ru content lowers the thermal decomposition temperature.
Limited atomic diffusion and initial atomic distributions in the secondary-heating nanoframework determine ultimate phase homogeneity.
A higher Ru fraction reduces the effective reduction temperature.
A reduced effective reduction temperature promotes faster and more uniform precursor decomposition.
Faster and more uniform precursor decomposition promotes more homogeneous alloy nucleation.
Lower Ru content slows reduction kinetics.
Slower reduction kinetics permit phase separation and elemental segregation.
Nanoscopic mixing during secondary heating mediates formation of a single-phase solid solution.
An optimized Pt–Ru ratio will improve single-phase crystallographic homogeneity.
An optimized Pt–Ru ratio will produce more uniform particle morphology and elemental distributions.
Ratios outside the optimal Pt–Ru range will produce detectable phase separation or elemental segregation relative to the baseline.
Conventional synthesis without deliberate Pt–Ru adjustment or secondary-heating control frequently yields mixed phases, elemental segregation, and inconsistent morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies only within a Pt–Ru composition and heating window that permits sufficient mobility while avoiding over-diffusion.
Outside the proposed composition or heating window, complete phase decomposition or uncontrolled re-agglomeration may dominate.

contradictions.description: The design says the overall composition is fixed while the Pt–Ru composition ratio is systematically varied. Changing that elemental ratio necessarily changes the composition unless compensating changes to other elements are defined.
